points.title: です
structure: Noun + です
な-adjective + です
い-adjective + です
points.explanation:
です goes at the end of a sentence and turns it into a polite statement that something *is* something. It is the backbone of basic Japanese: 学生です means "(I) am a student."

です never changes for person or number: the same word covers I, you, she and they. After nouns and な-adjectives it does the work of English "to be". After an い-adjective (おいしいです) it only adds politeness, because the adjective already contains the meaning "is".
nuances: です is the polite counterpart of だ. With strangers, teachers, coworkers and shop staff, です is the safe default.
The subject is usually dropped when it's obvious: 学生です alone can mean "I'm a student."
です has no meaning of existence ("there is") — that job belongs to あります / います.
common_mistakes: Adding です after a ます verb: 行きますです ✗. ます is already polite.
Using だ after an い-adjective: おいしいだ ✗. Say おいしい (casual) or おいしいです (polite).
Using です to say where something is located in the sense of "exists" (机の上に本です ✗ → 本があります).

points.title: は (topic)
structure: Topic + は + comment
points.explanation:
は marks the topic — what the sentence is about. Everything after は is a comment on that topic. In X は Y です, X is the topic and Y is what you're saying about it.

Often the topic is also the subject, but not always: は simply sets the frame, a bit like "Speaking of X…". As a particle it is written with the kana は but pronounced "wa".
nuances: Once a topic is established, speakers usually stop repeating it in following sentences.
は can carry a contrastive feel — "X, at least" or "X, as opposed to others" — which becomes very noticeable in negative sentences.
The "wa" pronunciation is a historical spelling that survives only in this particle (and in greetings like こんにちは).
common_mistakes: Writing わ for the particle: 私わ ✗ → 私は.
Treating は and が as interchangeable. は presents something as the topic; が points out or identifies it, often as new information.

comparisons.note: が marks the subject that exists or is being identified; は marks what the sentence is about.

points.title: か (question)
structure: Polite sentence + か
Question word … + か
points.explanation:
Add か to the end of a sentence and it becomes a question — the word order stays exactly the same. 学生です ("I'm a student") becomes 学生ですか ("Are you a student?").

Question words such as 何 (what), どこ (where) and いくら (how much) sit where the answer would go, and か still closes the sentence. In standard writing a か-question ends with 。 rather than ?.
nuances: Your intonation usually rises on か, just like an English yes/no question.
In casual speech people often drop か and just raise their voice. Plain だ + か can sound blunt or rough.
そうですか said with falling intonation isn't really a question — it means "I see."
common_mistakes: Rearranging the sentence like English. Japanese keeps the statement's order and adds か.
Adding ? after か isn't wrong in casual text, but 。 is standard in formal writing.

points.title: これ／それ／あれ／どれ
points.meaning: this one / that one / that one over there / which one
structure: これ / それ / あれ + は …
どれ + が … ですか
points.explanation:
これ, それ and あれ stand in for a thing, like English "this one" and "that one". The first syllable tells you where the thing is: こ- is close to the speaker, そ- is close to the listener, あ- is away from both of you, and ど- asks which one.

These words stand alone. They are never followed directly by a noun — that is the job of この／その／あの, the next lesson.
nuances: The こ／そ／あ／ど pattern runs through many words: この, ここ, こちら, こう… Learn it once and it keeps paying off.
Question words can't be the topic, so どれ takes が, not は: どれがあなたのですか.
common_mistakes: Putting a noun right after これ: これ本 ✗ → この本.
Using どれ to choose between just two things. For two options Japanese uses どちら.

examples.english: This is a book.

points.title: の (linking nouns)
points.meaning: 's / of — the first noun describes the second
structure: Noun₁ + の + Noun₂
points.explanation:
の joins two nouns so that the first describes the second. The most common case is possession — 私の本 "my book" — but it covers many relationships: origin (日本の車, "a Japanese car"), subject area (日本語の先生, "a Japanese teacher"), location (東京の大学, "a university in Tokyo").

The core idea: Noun₁ の Noun₂ is "the Noun₂ connected with Noun₁". The main noun always comes last.
nuances: You can chain の: 私の友だちの車 "my friend's car".
When the second noun is obvious, it can be dropped: これは私のです "This is mine."
の works the same at every politeness level.
common_mistakes: Reversing the order: 本の私 ✗. The owner or describer comes first: 私の本.
Putting の between an い-adjective and a noun: 大きいの車 ✗ → 大きい車.

points.title: この／その／あの／どの
points.meaning: this / that / that … over there / which + noun
structure: この / その / あの / どの + Noun
points.explanation: この, その, あの and どの follow the same distance rule as これ／それ／あれ／どれ, but they can't stand alone: a noun must come right after them. この本 is "this book", あの人 is "that person over there", どの部屋 is "which room".
nuances: あの人 is the neutral way to say "that person"; あの方 is the polite version.
あの… on its own is also a hesitation word, like "um…" at the start of a sentence.
common_mistakes: Using この without a noun: このは私のです ✗ → これは私のです.
Using これ before a noun: これ本 ✗ → この本.

points.title: さん／くん／ちゃん／様
points.meaning: name suffixes — how to address people
structure: Family / given name + さん (general polite)
+ くん (boys, juniors) / ちゃん (children, close friends)
+ 様 (very polite: customers, letters)
+ 先生 (teachers, doctors)
points.explanation:
Japanese attaches a suffix to people's names. さん is the all-purpose polite one: 田中さん. くん is for boys and younger men, or juniors at work; ちゃん is affectionate, for children, close friends and pets. 様 is very polite, used for customers and in letters: 山田様. Titles like 先生 work as suffixes too: 佐藤先生.

Never use a suffix on your own name.
nuances: With close friends you can drop the suffix (呼び捨て), but that's intimate.
Job titles can replace a name: 社長, 部長, 先生.
common_mistakes: Adding さん to yourself: 私はジョンさんです ✗ → 私はジョンです.
Using ちゃん with a superior — it's too familiar.

points.title: ここ／そこ／あそこ／どこ
structure: ここ / そこ / あそこ + は + Place + です
Thing + は + どこですか
points.explanation:
ここ, そこ, あそこ and どこ are place words on the same こ／そ／あ／ど pattern: ここ is where the speaker is, そこ is near the listener, あそこ is away from both, and どこ asks where.

They work like nouns, so particles attach directly: ここで, あそこに, どこへ.
nuances: こちら／そちら／あちら／どちら are the polite versions, often used by shop staff: お手洗いはあちらです.
Note the irregular あそこ — not あこ.
common_mistakes: Saying あこ instead of あそこ.
Leaving out the particle in a verb sentence: ここ食べます ✗ → ここで食べます.

points.title: も
points.meaning: also, too; (with a negative) not … either
structure: Noun + も (replaces は, が or を)
Noun + other particle + も (にも, でも …)
points.explanation:
も means "also" or "too". It takes the place of は, が or を: instead of 私は学生です, say 私も学生です — "I'm a student too."

も attaches right after the word that is "also" true. In a negative sentence it means "not … either". Other particles such as に and で stay put and も is added after them (ここにも, そこでも).
nuances: X も Y も means "both X and Y", or "neither X nor Y" with a negative verb.
Question word + も + negative gives total negation — 何もありません "there's nothing at all" — a pattern you'll meet later.
common_mistakes: Stacking は and も: 私はも ✗. も replaces は.
Putting も at the end like English "too": 学生ですも ✗. It goes right after the word it adds to.

comparisons.note: は sets up a topic; も says the same comment applies to this topic too.

points.title: じゃありません / ではありません
points.meaning: is not (polite negative of です)
structure: Noun + じゃありません
な-adjective + じゃありません
More formal: … ではありません
Conversational: … じゃないです
points.explanation:
To say politely that something is not X, replace です with じゃありません. じゃ is the spoken contraction of では, so ではありません is slightly more formal and common in writing, while じゃありません is typical in conversation. じゃないです is another polite option you'll hear constantly in everyday speech.

All of these work with nouns and な-adjectives.
nuances: い-adjectives do not use this pattern: 高いじゃありません ✗. They conjugate on their own (高くないです) — covered later.
The は in では is the topic particle, pronounced "wa".
common_mistakes: Using じゃありません after an い-adjective (おいしいじゃありません ✗).
Writing でわ instead of では.

comparisons.note: です is the affirmative; じゃありません is its negative.

points.title: でした／じゃありませんでした
points.meaning: was / was not (polite past of です)
structure: Noun / な-adjective + でした
Noun / な-adjective + じゃありませんでした
Conversational: … じゃなかったです
points.explanation:
でした is the past of です: 学生でした, "I was a student." For the negative past, add でした to じゃありません: 学生じゃありませんでした, "I wasn't a student."

Like です, these follow nouns and な-adjectives. い-adjectives have their own past forms, covered in a later lesson.
nuances: じゃなかったです is a common, slightly more relaxed polite negative past.
ではありませんでした is the more formal version, common in writing.
common_mistakes: Using でした after an い-adjective: 高いでした ✗ → 高かったです.
じゃないでした ✗ — say じゃありませんでした or じゃなかったです.

points.title: い-adjectives
points.meaning: describing words ending in い — present and negative
structure: い-adjective + Noun (高い本)
Noun は + い-adjective + です
Negative: drop い → くない(です) / くありません
Irregular: いい → よくない
points.explanation:
い-adjectives end in い and go straight in front of a noun: 高い本, "an expensive book". At the end of a sentence, add です to be polite: この本は高いです.

To make one negative, replace the final い with くない: 高い → 高くない, "not expensive". Politely: 高くないです or 高くありません. The one irregular adjective is いい (good), whose forms are built on よい: よくない.
nuances: 高くないです and 高くありません are both polite; ありません sounds slightly more formal.
A few words ending in い are really な-adjectives, notably きれい and きらい.
common_mistakes: Negating with じゃない: 高いじゃない ✗ → 高くない.
いくない ✗ → よくない.

points.title: な-adjectives
points.meaning: describing words that take な before a noun
structure: な-adjective + な + Noun (静かな町)
Noun は + な-adjective + です
Negative: な-adjective + じゃありません
points.explanation:
な-adjectives behave a lot like nouns. At the end of a sentence they take です directly: この町は静かです. When they come before a noun, though, they need な: 静かな町, "a quiet town".

Their negative and past forms are the same as a noun's: 静かじゃありません, 静かでした.
nuances: Common な-adjectives: 静か, きれい, 元気, 有名, 好き, 便利, 親切, 大丈夫.
きれい looks like an い-adjective but isn't: きれいな花, きれいじゃない.
common_mistakes: Dropping な before a noun: 静か町 ✗ → 静かな町.
Keeping な at the end of a sentence: 静かなです ✗ → 静かです.
Treating きれい as an い-adjective: きれくない ✗ → きれいじゃない.

points.title: い-adjective past
structure: drop い → かった(です)
drop い → くなかった(です)
いい → よかった / よくなかった
points.explanation:
い-adjectives carry their own tense. Replace the final い with かった for the past: 高い → 高かった, "was expensive". For the negative past, use くなかった: 高くなかった, "wasn't expensive". Add です to be polite: 高かったです.

いい again switches to よ: よかった, よくなかった.
nuances: よかった on its own is a very common reaction: "Thank goodness" or "I'm glad."
くありませんでした is an equally polite, slightly more formal negative past.
common_mistakes: 高いでした ✗ — the adjective takes the past tense, not です: 高かったです.
いかった ✗ → よかった.

points.title: 〜の (the … one)
points.meaning: the one — standing in for a noun
structure: い-adjective + の (赤いの)
な-adjective + な + の (静かなの)
Noun + の (…'s one: 私の)
points.explanation:
の can stand in for a noun you don't need to repeat, like English "one": 赤いのをください, "The red one, please." With な-adjectives, keep な: もっと静かなのがいいです.

After a noun it means "…'s": この傘は私のです, "This umbrella is mine."
nuances: It's extremely common when shopping and choosing.
Sometimes もの is used instead, a little more formally.
common_mistakes: Dropping な: 静かのがいい ✗ → 静かなのがいい.
Adding の after これ／それ: これのをください ✗ → これをください.

points.title: ね
structure: Sentence + ね
points.explanation:
ね at the end of a sentence invites the listener to share your view, like "isn't it?" or "right?". Use it when you expect the other person already knows or agrees: いい天気ですね, "Nice weather, isn't it?"

It softens what you say and makes conversation feel warm.
nuances: With rising intonation, ね checks a fact: 明日ですね？ "It's tomorrow, right?"
Using ね a lot sounds chatty, but using none at all can sound cold in conversation.
common_mistakes: Using ね for news the listener doesn't know — that's the job of よ.
Adding ね to formal writing, where it sounds too conversational.

comparisons.note: ね assumes shared knowledge; よ tells the listener something new.

points.title: よ
points.meaning: you know — new information or emphasis
structure: Sentence + よ
points.explanation: よ at the end of a sentence marks information the listener probably doesn't have, or something you want them to notice: この店は安いですよ, "This shop is cheap, you know." It adds confidence, a bit like "you know" or "I'm telling you".
nuances: よね combines the two: "…right? (I'm fairly sure)".
A strong よ toward a superior can sound like you're correcting them.
common_mistakes: Using よ about something you both see: いい天気ですよ sounds like you're announcing the weather. ね is usually what you want.
Using よ in formal writing.

comparisons.note: よ tells the listener something new; ね assumes they already agree.

points.title: Verb-ます
points.meaning: polite non-past verb: do / will do
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ます
う-verbs: 行く → 行きます, 飲む → 飲みます
る-verbs: 食べる → 食べます, 見る → 見ます
Irregular: する → します, 来る → 来ます (きます)
points.explanation:
ます is the polite ending for verbs. It covers both habits and future actions — Japanese has no separate future tense, so 行きます can mean "I go" or "I'll go", and context decides.

To build it, find the ます-stem. For る-verbs, drop る (食べる → 食べ). For う-verbs, change the final u-sound to its i-sound (飲む → 飲み, 書く → 書き). Then add ます. The two irregular verbs are する → します and 来る → 来ます.
nuances: The form doesn't change for the subject: I, you and they all 行きます.
Use ます forms with people you don't know well; with close friends you'd use the dictionary form.
common_mistakes: Treating a う-verb that ends in る as a る-verb: 帰る → 帰ります, not 帰ます. Watch out for 帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る.
Using ます for something happening right this moment. "I'm eating (now)" needs 〜ています, covered later.

points.title: Verb-ません
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ません
points.explanation:
Swap ます for ません to make a polite negative: 行きます → 行きません, "I don't go" or "I won't go". Like ます, it covers both habits and the future.

Every verb follows the same rule, including the irregulars: しません, 来ません (きません).
nuances: In relaxed polite speech you'll also hear the plain negative + です (行かないです). ません sounds a little more proper.
A natural negative answer repeats the verb: 行きますか → いいえ、行きません.
common_mistakes: Skipping the stem: 行くません ✗ → 行きません.
Mixing up 来ません (きません, "won't come") with 着ません (きません, "won't wear") — same sound, different verbs.

comparisons.note: ます is the affirmative; ません is its negative.

points.title: を
structure: Noun + を + transitive verb
points.explanation:
を marks the direct object — the thing an action is done to. In パンを食べます ("I eat bread"), the bread is what gets eaten, so it takes を.

を comes right after the object, and the verb usually follows at the end of the sentence. It is written を but pronounced the same as お.
nuances: With movement verbs, を can also mark the space you move through (公園を歩きます, "walk through the park") — a later lesson.
In casual speech を is often dropped: パン食べる？
common_mistakes: Typing お for the particle — it must be を. (In romaji, type "wo".)
Using を with 好き or わかる: 猫を好きです ✗ → 猫が好きです.
Using を for the destination of 行く: 学校を行きます ✗ → 学校へ / に行きます.

points.title: Noun をください
points.meaning: please give me … (asking for things, ordering)
structure: Noun + をください
Noun + を + number + ください
points.explanation:
Noun をください is the simplest polite way to ask for something: 水をください, "Water, please." It's what you say at shops, stations and restaurants.

To say how many, put the number between を and ください: りんごを三つください, "Three apples, please."
nuances: In casual speech を is often dropped: これください.
〜をお願いします is a slightly softer alternative, very common when ordering.
common_mistakes: Putting the number before the noun: 三つのりんごをください sounds odd when ordering → りんごを三つください.
Using Noun をください for actions. Asking someone to do something needs the て-form (待ってください), covered later.

points.title: に (time)
points.meaning: at / on / in — a specific point in time
structure: Time + に + verb
points.explanation: に after a time expression marks when an action happens: 七時に起きます, "I get up at seven." Use it with clock times, dates, days of the week, months and years — anything that pins the action to a specific point on the clock or calendar.
nuances: Relative time words — 今日, 明日, 毎日, 毎朝, 今, 来週 — do NOT take に. Say 明日行きます, not 明日に行きます.
Days of the week work both with and without に; with に it sounds a little more precise.
When several time words stack, the largest comes first and only the last one takes に: 日曜日の九時に.
common_mistakes: Adding に to relative time words: 毎朝に ✗.
Using で for a time: 七時で ✗ → 七時に.

points.title: へ / に (destination)
points.meaning: to — the direction or destination of movement
structure: Place + へ / に + 行きます・来ます・帰ります
points.explanation:
With movement verbs — 行く (go), 来る (come), 帰る (go home) — both へ and に mark where you're heading. へ (pronounced "e") leans toward direction, "toward"; に leans toward the arrival point, "to".

In everyday use they are mostly interchangeable: 学校へ行きます and 学校に行きます both mean "I go to school."
nuances: に is more common in conversation; へ feels a little more written or directional.
Only へ can take の to modify a noun: 母への手紙 "a letter to my mother" (にの is impossible).
common_mistakes: Writing え for the particle — it must be へ. (In romaji, type "he".)
Using を for a destination: 学校を行きます ✗.
Using で for a destination: で marks where an action happens, not where you go.

comparisons.note: Same particle に, different job: time point vs. destination.
で marks where an action takes place; へ / に mark where you move to.

points.title: を (through / out of)
points.meaning: along, through, out of — a place you move through or leave
structure: Place + を + 歩く / 走る / 渡る / 散歩する (through, along)
Place + を + 出る / 降りる / 卒業する (out of)
points.explanation:
With movement verbs, を can mark the space you move through: 毎朝公園を散歩します, "I take a walk in the park every morning." この橋を渡ってください, "Please cross this bridge."

With verbs of leaving, it marks the place you leave: 七時に家を出ます, "I leave home at seven." 電車を降ります, "get off the train".
nuances: 公園で走る is running as an activity at the park; 公園を走る is running through or around it.
卒業する takes を too: 大学を卒業しました.
common_mistakes: Using に with 降りる: 電車に降ります ✗ → 電車を降ります.
家から出ます is possible, but 家を出ます is the natural everyday phrase.

comparisons.note: Same particle: パンを食べる marks the object; 公園を歩く marks the path.

points.title: で (place of action)
points.meaning: at / in — where an action takes place
structure: Place + で + action verb
points.explanation: で marks the place where an action happens: 図書館で勉強します, "I study at the library." Think of it as the stage on which the activity is performed. It goes with action verbs — eat, study, work, buy, play and so on.
nuances: For where something simply exists (あります / います), use に, not で. This contrast is one of the key N5 distinctions.
で has other uses too — for example a means or tool (バスで, "by bus") — covered in a later lesson.
common_mistakes: Using に with an action: 図書館に勉強します ✗ → 図書館で.
Using で with あります / います: 部屋で猫がいます ✗ → 部屋に.

comparisons.note: Existence takes に (部屋に猫がいます); actions take で (部屋で勉強します).
へ / に mark where you go; で marks where you do something.

points.title: ました / ませんでした
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ました
Verb (ます-stem) + ませんでした
points.explanation:
To put a ます verb into the past, change ます to ました: 食べます → 食べました, "ate". For the negative past, add でした to ません: 食べませんでした, "didn't eat".

The rule is the same for every verb, irregulars included (しました, 来ました).
nuances: ました also expresses completion, where English might use "have done": もう食べました, "I've already eaten."
Answer a 〜ましたか question with the same verb: はい、行きました / いいえ、行きませんでした.
common_mistakes: Saying ませんました ✗ — the negative past is ませんでした.
Using the present when English uses "have done": "I've finished" is 終わりました.

comparisons.note: ます / ません are non-past; ました / ませんでした are past.

examples.japanese: 昨日、映画を見ました。
examples.furigana: {昨日|きのう}、{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ました。
examples.english: I watched a movie yesterday.

examples.japanese: 朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.furigana: {朝|あさ}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't eat breakfast.

valid_alternatives.note: 食べなかったです is also polite, but more casual. This review wants ませんでした.

examples.hint: 食べる (to eat) → polite negative past

examples.japanese: 先週、京都へ行きました。
examples.furigana: {先週|せんしゅう}、{京都|きょうと}へ{行|い}きました。
examples.english: I went to Kyoto last week.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは来ませんでした。
examples.furigana: {田中|たなか}さんは{来|き}ませんでした。
examples.english: Tanaka-san didn't come.

valid_alternatives.note: 来なかったです is also polite, but more casual. This review wants ませんでした.
こなかったです is also polite, but more casual. This review wants ませんでした.

examples.hint: 来る (to come) → polite negative past

examples.japanese: 昨日の夜、十二時に寝ました。

examples.japanese: 週末は勉強しませんでした。

valid_alternatives.note: しなかったです is also polite, but more casual. This review wants ませんでした.

examples.hint: する (to do) → polite negative past

points.title: と (and)
points.meaning: and — joining nouns in a complete list
structure: Noun₁ + と + Noun₂
Noun₁ + と + Noun₂ + と + Noun₃
points.explanation:
と joins nouns: パンと卵, "bread and eggs". It implies the list is complete — these things and nothing else.

と only joins nouns. It can't link verbs, adjectives or whole sentences; those use other forms (the て-form, そして) that come later.
nuances: For an open-ended list ("things like A and B"), use や instead.
With three or more items, と can go between each one: パンと卵と牛乳.
common_mistakes: Joining verbs with と: 食べましたと寝ました ✗ → 食べて寝ました.
Joining adjectives with と: 安いとおいしい ✗ → 安くておいしい.

comparisons.note: と gives the full list; や gives a few examples.
Same particle, different job: "and" between nouns vs. "with" a person.

examples.japanese: パンと卵を買いました。
examples.furigana: パンと{卵|たまご}を{買|か}いました。
examples.english: I bought bread and eggs.

valid_alternatives.note: や is grammatical but implies there were other things too. This review wants the complete-list と.

examples.japanese: 兄と姉がいます。
examples.furigana: {兄|あに}と{姉|あね}がいます。
examples.english: I have an older brother and an older sister.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本とペンがあります。
examples.furigana: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}に{本|ほん}とペンがあります。
examples.english: There's a book and a pen on the desk.

valid_alternatives.note: や is grammatical but implies there are other things too. This review wants the complete-list と.

examples.japanese: 月曜日と木曜日に日本語の授業があります。
examples.furigana: {月曜日|げつようび}と{木曜日|もくようび}に{日本語|にほんご}の{授業|じゅぎょう}があります。
examples.english: I have Japanese class on Mondays and Thursdays.

examples.japanese: 朝はいつもコーヒーとパンです。
examples.furigana: {朝|あさ}はいつもコーヒーとパンです。
examples.english: In the morning I always have coffee and bread.

points.title: や／など
points.meaning: things like A and B — a partial list
structure: Noun₁ + や + Noun₂
Noun₁ + や + Noun₂ + など
points.explanation:
や joins nouns like と, but it signals that the list is only a sample: りんごやバナナ, "apples, bananas and so on". You name a couple of examples and imply there are others.

など after the last item makes the "and so on" explicit: りんごやバナナなど.
nuances: など can also follow a single noun to mean "things like…": 本などを読みます.
In casual speech, とか does a similar job to や.
common_mistakes: Using や when you mean an exact, complete list — use と.
Joining verbs or sentences with や ✗; it's for nouns only.

comparisons.note: や gives examples; と gives the complete list.

examples.japanese: 冷蔵庫に卵や牛乳があります。
examples.furigana: {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}に{卵|たまご}や{牛乳|ぎゅうにゅう}があります。
examples.english: There are eggs, milk and so on in the fridge.

valid_alternatives.note: と is grammatical but says these are the only things. や implies there are others.

examples.japanese: 休みの日は映画や買い物に行きます。
examples.furigana: {休|やす}みの{日|ひ}は{映画|えいが}や{買|か}い{物|もの}に{行|い}きます。
examples.english: On days off I go to movies, go shopping and so on.

valid_alternatives.note: と is grammatical but says these are the only things. や implies there are others.

examples.japanese: 机の上にペンや本などがあります。
examples.furigana: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}にペンや{本|ほん}などがあります。
examples.english: There are pens, books and such on the desk.

examples.japanese: 京都や奈良に行きたいです。
examples.furigana: {京都|きょうと}や{奈良|なら}に{行|い}きたいです。
examples.english: I want to go to places like Kyoto and Nara.

valid_alternatives.note: と is grammatical but says these are the only things. や implies there are others.

examples.japanese: 肉や野菜を買いました。
examples.furigana: {肉|にく}や{野菜|やさい}を{買|か}いました。
examples.english: I bought meat, vegetables and other things.

valid_alternatives.note: と is grammatical but says these are the only things. や implies there are others.

points.title: と (with)
structure: Person + と + verb
Person + と + 一緒に + verb
points.explanation:
と after a person marks who you do something with: 友だちと映画を見ます, "I watch a movie with a friend." Adding 一緒に (together) makes it explicit: 友だちと一緒に.

Some verbs need a partner by nature and always take と: 結婚する (marry), けんかする (quarrel).
nuances: With 会う (meet), both に and と work: 友だちに会う focuses on going to see them; 友だちと会う sounds more mutual.
For tools ("with a pen"), use で, not と.
common_mistakes: Using と for tools: ペンと書きます ✗ → ペンで書きます.
Using を with 結婚する: 田中さんを結婚しました ✗ → 田中さんと結婚しました.

examples.japanese: 友だちと映画を見ました。
examples.furigana: {友|とも}だちと{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ました。
examples.english: I watched a movie with a friend.

examples.japanese: 毎週、母と電話で話します。
examples.furigana: {毎週|まいしゅう}、{母|はは}と{電話|でんわ}で{話|はな}します。
examples.english: I talk with my mother on the phone every week.

examples.japanese: 姉は去年アメリカ人と結婚しました。
examples.furigana: {姉|あね}は{去年|きょねん}アメリカ{人|じん}と{結婚|けっこん}しました。
examples.english: My older sister married an American last year.

examples.japanese: 家族と一緒に旅行します。
examples.furigana: {家族|かぞく}と{一緒|いっしょ}に{旅行|りょこう}します。
examples.english: I'm traveling together with my family.

examples.japanese: だれと行きますか。
examples.furigana: だれと{行|い}きますか。
examples.english: Who are you going with?

points.title: で (means)
points.meaning: by / with / in — the means or tool
structure: Means / tool / language + で + verb
points.explanation:
で after a tool, method, language or means of transport says how you do something: バスで行きます "go by bus", はしで食べます "eat with chopsticks", 日本語で話します "speak in Japanese".

It's the same particle as で for the place of an action — the noun makes clear which meaning you want.
nuances: Going on foot is special: 歩いて行きます, not 足で行きます.
Payment works the same way: カードで払います, "pay by card".
common_mistakes: Using と for a tool: はしと食べます ✗ → はしで食べます.
Using で for walking: 足で行きます ✗ → 歩いて行きます.

comparisons.note: Same particle: 図書館で is where; バスで is how.

examples.japanese: 毎日バスで学校へ行きます。
examples.furigana: {毎日|まいにち}バスで{学校|がっこう}へ{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I go to school by bus every day.

examples.japanese: はしで食べます。
examples.furigana: はしで{食|た}べます。
examples.english: I eat with chopsticks.

examples.japanese: 日本語で手紙を書きました。
examples.furigana: {日本語|にほんご}で{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}きました。
examples.english: I wrote a letter in Japanese.

examples.japanese: 電話で予約しました。
examples.furigana: {電話|でんわ}で{予約|よやく}しました。
examples.english: I made a reservation by phone.

examples.japanese: 京都へは新幹線で行きます。
examples.furigana: {京都|きょうと}へは{新幹線|しんかんせん}で{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I'll go to Kyoto by shinkansen.

points.title: で (total / who together)
points.meaning: for (a quantity), altogether, by oneself / together
structure: Quantity + で + price (三つで五百円)
全部で (altogether)
一人で / みんなで / 二人で
points.explanation:
で after a quantity marks the unit a price or result applies to: りんごは三つで五百円です, "The apples are 500 yen for three." 全部でいくらですか, "How much is it altogether?"

With people, it says who does something — alone or together: 一人で行きました, みんなで写真を撮りましょう.
nuances: 一人で means "by myself"; 二人で means "the two of us together".
It's the same particle as で for place and means; context sorts it out.
common_mistakes: Using に: 三つに五百円 ✗ → 三つで五百円.
Using と for "altogether": 全部と ✗ → 全部で.

examples.japanese: りんごは三つで五百円です。
examples.furigana: りんごは{三|みっ}つで{五百円|ごひゃくえん}です。
examples.english: The apples are 500 yen for three.

examples.japanese: 全部でいくらですか。
examples.furigana: {全部|ぜんぶ}でいくらですか。
examples.english: How much is it altogether?

examples.japanese: 週末は一人で映画を見に行きました。
examples.furigana: {週末|しゅうまつ}は{一人|ひとり}で{映画|えいが}を{見|み}に{行|い}きました。
examples.english: At the weekend I went to see a movie by myself.

examples.japanese: みんなで写真を撮りましょう。
examples.furigana: みんなで{写真|しゃしん}を{撮|と}りましょう。
examples.english: Let's all take a photo together.

examples.japanese: 家族四人で旅行しました。
examples.furigana: {家族|かぞく}{四人|よにん}で{旅行|りょこう}しました。
examples.english: The four of us in my family went on a trip together.

points.title: に (target person)
points.meaning: to — the person an action is directed at
structure: Person + に + 会う / 電話する / 聞く
Person + に + Thing + を + 書く / 貸す / あげる
points.explanation:
に marks the person an action is aimed at: 友だちに手紙を書きます "write a letter to a friend", 先生に聞きます "ask the teacher".

Some verbs always take に for their partner: 会う (meet), 電話する (phone), 質問する (ask a question).
nuances: You'll meet this に again with giving and receiving verbs (あげる, もらう) at N4.
友だちに会う (meet a friend) and 友だちと会う (meet up with a friend) are both fine.
common_mistakes: Using を with 会う: 友だちを会います ✗ → 友だちに会います.
Using へ for a person. へ is for places and directions.

examples.japanese: 駅で友だちに会いました。
examples.furigana: {駅|えき}で{友|とも}だちに{会|あ}いました。
examples.english: I met a friend at the station.

valid_alternatives.note: 友だちと会う is also fine. This review practises に with 会う.

examples.japanese: 母に電話しました。
examples.furigana: {母|はは}に{電話|でんわ}しました。
examples.english: I phoned my mother.

examples.japanese: 先生に質問しました。
examples.furigana: {先生|せんせい}に{質問|しつもん}しました。
examples.english: I asked the teacher a question.

examples.japanese: 毎月、祖母に手紙を書きます。
examples.furigana: {毎月|まいつき}、{祖母|そぼ}に{手紙|てがみ}を{書|か}きます。
examples.english: Every month I write a letter to my grandmother.

examples.japanese: 友だちに本を貸しました。
examples.furigana: {友|とも}だちに{本|ほん}を{貸|か}しました。
examples.english: I lent a book to a friend.

points.title: から／まで
structure: Time / place + から (from)
Time / place + まで (until, as far as)
A + から + B + まで
points.explanation:
から marks a starting point and まで an end point, for both time and place: 九時から五時まで "from nine to five", 東京から大阪まで "from Tokyo to Osaka".

Each can also stand alone: 何時までですか, "Until what time?"
nuances: です can follow directly: 授業は九時からです.
までに (by, no later than) is different from まで (until) — you'll meet it at N4.
common_mistakes: Using に for a starting time: 九時に五時まで ✗ → 九時から五時まで.
Mixing up まで (until) and までに (by a deadline).

examples.japanese: 銀行は九時から三時までです。
examples.furigana: {銀行|ぎんこう}は{九時|くじ}から{三時|さんじ}までです。
examples.english: The bank is open from nine to three.

examples.japanese: 授業は月曜日から金曜日までです。
examples.furigana: {授業|じゅぎょう}は{月曜日|げつようび}から{金曜日|きんようび}までです。
examples.english: Classes run Monday to Friday.

examples.japanese: 家から駅まで歩きます。
examples.furigana: {家|いえ}から{駅|えき}まで{歩|ある}きます。
examples.english: I walk from home to the station.

examples.japanese: 昨日は夜十一時まで働きました。
examples.furigana: {昨日|きのう}は{夜|よる}{十一時|じゅういちじ}まで{働|はたら}きました。
examples.english: Yesterday I worked until eleven at night.

examples.japanese: 東京から大阪まで新幹線で行きます。
examples.furigana: {東京|とうきょう}から{大阪|おおさか}まで{新幹線|しんかんせん}で{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I'm going from Tokyo to Osaka by shinkansen.

points.title: が あります / います
structure: Place + に + Thing + が + あります (non-living things)
Place + に + Person / Animal + が + います (living beings)
Thing + は + Place + に + あります / います
points.explanation:
あります and います both mean "there is" or "exists". The difference is what exists: あります is for things that don't move on their own — objects, buildings, plants, events. います is for people and animals.

The thing that exists is marked with が, and its location with に: 部屋に猫がいます, "There's a cat in the room." あります also expresses having something: 車があります, "I have a car."
nuances: When the thing is already the topic, turn it around: 猫は部屋にいます, "The cat is in the room."
The negatives are ありません and いません. The ありません in じゃありません is this same verb.
A few edge cases bend the rule (a taxi with a driver waiting can take います), but the living / non-living test works almost all the time.
common_mistakes: Using あります for people or pets: 犬があります ✗ → 犬がいます.
Marking the location with で: 公園で子どもがいます ✗ → 公園に.
Using です to say something exists: 机の上に本です ✗ → 本があります.

comparisons.note: Location of existence takes に; location of an action takes で.
が introduces what exists; は talks about something already known.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本があります。
examples.furigana: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}に{本|ほん}があります。
examples.english: There's a book on the desk.
examples.hint: there is — あります or います?

examples.japanese: 庭に猫がいます。
examples.furigana: {庭|にわ}に{猫|ねこ}がいます。
examples.english: There's a cat in the garden.
examples.hint: there is — あります or います?

examples.japanese: 教室に学生が三人います。
examples.furigana: {教室|きょうしつ}に{学生|がくせい}が{三人|さんにん}います。
examples.english: There are three students in the classroom.
examples.hint: there are — あります or います?

examples.japanese: 駅の近くに銀行がありますか。
examples.furigana: {駅|えき}の{近|ちか}くに{銀行|ぎんこう}がありますか。
examples.english: Is there a bank near the station?
examples.hint: is there — あります or います?

examples.japanese: 私は車がありません。
examples.furigana: {私|わたし}は{車|くるま}がありません。
examples.english: I don't have a car.

valid_alternatives.note: ないです is also polite, but more casual. This review wants ありません.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは今どこにいますか。
examples.furigana: {田中|たなか}さんは{今|いま}どこにいますか。
examples.english: Where is Tanaka-san now?
examples.hint: is (located) — あります or います?

points.title: が 好き／上手／わかる
points.meaning: が marks what you like, are good at, or understand
structure: Person + は + Thing + が + 好き / きらい
Person + は + Thing + が + 上手 / 下手
Person + は + Thing + が + わかる
points.explanation:
With words for liking, skill and understanding, the thing is marked with が, not を: 私は猫が好きです "I like cats", 田中さんは料理が上手です "Tanaka-san is good at cooking", 日本語がわかります "I understand Japanese".

The person usually takes は, so the full pattern is Person は Thing が ….
nuances: 上手 is praise for others; about yourself, 得意 sounds less boastful.
大好き (love) and 大きらい (hate) follow the same pattern.
common_mistakes: Using を: 猫を好きです ✗ → 猫が好きです.
Using を with わかる: 日本語をわかります ✗ → 日本語がわかります.

examples.japanese: 私は猫が好きです。
examples.furigana: {私|わたし}は{猫|ねこ}が{好|す}きです。
examples.english: I like cats.

examples.japanese: 田中さんは料理が上手です。
examples.furigana: {田中|たなか}さんは{料理|りょうり}が{上手|じょうず}です。
examples.english: Tanaka-san is good at cooking.

examples.japanese: 英語がわかりますか。
examples.furigana: {英語|えいご}がわかりますか。
examples.english: Do you understand English?

examples.japanese: 弟は野菜がきらいです。
examples.furigana: {弟|おとうと}は{野菜|やさい}がきらいです。
examples.english: My younger brother doesn't like vegetables.

examples.japanese: 私は歌が下手です。
examples.furigana: {私|わたし}は{歌|うた}が{下手|へた}です。
examples.english: I'm bad at singing.

points.title: Question word + が
points.meaning: who / what / which … as the subject of a question
structure: だれ / 何 / どれ / どこ + が + …
Answer: Noun + が + …
points.explanation:
When a question word is the subject, it takes が, never は: だれが来ましたか, "Who came?" The answer keeps が: 田中さんが来ました.

The reason: は marks something already known, and a question word is by definition the unknown part.
nuances: The same logic gives どれが and どの本が.
In the answer, が highlights the new information that fills the gap.
common_mistakes: だれは来ましたか ✗ → だれが来ましたか.
Answering "Who's going?" with 私は行きます sounds off → 私が行きます.

examples.japanese: だれが来ましたか。
examples.furigana: だれが{来|き}ましたか。
examples.english: Who came?
examples.hint: subject marker after a question word

examples.japanese: 冷蔵庫に何がありますか。
examples.furigana: {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}に{何|なに}がありますか。
examples.english: What's in the fridge?
examples.hint: subject marker after a question word

examples.japanese: 私が行きます。
examples.furigana: {私|わたし}が{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I'll go. (answering "Who'll go?")

valid_alternatives.note: 私は行きます is grammatical, but in answer to "who?" the new information takes が.

examples.japanese: どれが田中さんのかばんですか。
examples.furigana: どれが{田中|たなか}さんのかばんですか。
examples.english: Which one is Tanaka-san's bag?
examples.hint: subject marker after a question word

examples.japanese: どこが痛いですか。
examples.furigana: どこが{痛|いた}いですか。
examples.english: Where does it hurt?
examples.hint: subject marker after a question word

points.title: が (subject / identifier)
points.meaning: marks the subject — new information, or "it's X (who/that)…"
structure: Noun + が + Verb / Adjective
AはBが〜 (A has a B that is…)
points.explanation:
が marks the subject of a sentence. Where は sets up a topic ("as for X…"), が points at exactly which thing does the action or has the quality: 田中さんが来ました, "Tanaka-san came" — or, answering "who came?", "it was Tanaka-san who came."

が is used for things you're noticing or reporting as new: 雨が降っています, "It's raining." In AはBが… sentences, は gives the topic and が the part being described: 象は鼻が長い, "Elephants have long trunks."
nuances: Question words take が, never は: 誰が来ましたか.
Inside a describing clause the subject takes が: 私が作ったケーキ, "the cake I made".
common_mistakes: Answering a が-question with は: 誰が行きますか → 私は行きます ✗ → 私が行きます.
Using は for something you've just noticed: あ、バスは来た ✗ → あ、バスが来た.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っています。
examples.furigana: {雨|あめ}が{降|ふ}っています。
examples.english: It's raining.

examples.japanese: 田中さんが来ました。
examples.furigana: {田中|たなか}さんが{来|き}ました。
examples.english: Tanaka-san came. / It was Tanaka-san who came.

examples.japanese: 私が払います。
examples.furigana: {私|わたし}が{払|はら}います。
examples.english: I'll pay. (I'm the one paying.)

examples.japanese: 象は鼻が長いです。
examples.furigana: {象|ぞう}は{鼻|はな}が{長|なが}いです。
examples.english: Elephants have long trunks.

examples.japanese: あ、バスが来ましたよ。
examples.furigana: あ、バスが{来|き}ましたよ。
examples.english: Oh, the bus is here.

points.title: か (or)
structure: Noun₁ + か + Noun₂
points.explanation: か between two nouns means "or": コーヒーか紅茶, "coffee or tea". It's the same か as the question marker — you can think of it as "A? or B?".
nuances: It can join more than two items: 月曜日か火曜日か水曜日.
To ask which one someone wants, combine it with どちら: コーヒーか紅茶、どちらがいいですか.
common_mistakes: Using と when you mean "or": コーヒーと紅茶を飲みます means both.
Leaving out the particle after the last noun: コーヒーか紅茶飲みます ✗ → コーヒーか紅茶を飲みます.

examples.japanese: コーヒーか紅茶を飲みます。
examples.furigana: コーヒーか{紅茶|こうちゃ}を{飲|の}みます。
examples.english: I'll have coffee or tea.

examples.japanese: 月曜日か火曜日に行きます。
examples.furigana: {月曜日|げつようび}か{火曜日|かようび}に{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I'll go on Monday or Tuesday.

examples.japanese: ペンか鉛筆で書きます。
examples.furigana: ペンか{鉛筆|えんぴつ}で{書|か}きます。
examples.english: I'll write with a pen or a pencil.

examples.japanese: 夏休みは北海道か沖縄に行きたいです。
examples.furigana: {夏休|なつやす}みは{北海道|ほっかいどう}か{沖縄|おきなわ}に{行|い}きたいです。
examples.english: For summer vacation I want to go to Hokkaido or Okinawa.

examples.japanese: 電車かバスで行きます。
examples.furigana: {電車|でんしゃ}かバスで{行|い}きます。
examples.english: I'll go by train or bus.

points.title: 何か／だれか／どこか
structure: Question word + か
何か / だれか / どこか / いつか
points.explanation:
Adding か to a question word turns it into an indefinite word: 何か "something", だれか "someone", どこか "somewhere", いつか "sometime".

が and を are usually dropped after these: 何か食べますか, "Will you eat something?" Other particles stay: どこかへ, だれかに.
nuances: 何か with rising intonation is a natural "Anything?" question.
いつか often carries a hopeful "someday" feeling.
common_mistakes: Confusing 何か (something) with 何が (what, as subject).
Using 何か with a negative to mean "nothing" — that needs 何も.

comparisons.note: 何か is "something"; 何も + negative is "nothing".

examples.japanese: 何か飲みますか。
examples.furigana: {何|なに}か{飲|の}みますか。
examples.english: Will you have something to drink?

examples.japanese: だれか来ましたか。
examples.furigana: だれか{来|き}ましたか。
examples.english: Did someone come?

examples.japanese: 週末はどこかへ行きましたか。
examples.furigana: {週末|しゅうまつ}はどこかへ{行|い}きましたか。
examples.english: Did you go anywhere over the weekend?

examples.japanese: いつか日本に住みたいです。
examples.furigana: いつか{日本|にほん}に{住|す}みたいです。
examples.english: I want to live in Japan someday.

examples.japanese: 机の上に何かありますか。
examples.furigana: {机|つくえ}の{上|うえ}に{何|なに}かありますか。
examples.english: Is there something on the desk?

points.title: 何も／だれも／どこも + negative
structure: Question word + も + negative
Question word + particle + も + negative (どこへも, だれにも)
points.explanation:
Question word + も with a negative verb means "not any": 何も食べません "I don't eat anything", だれもいません "There's no one here", どこへも行きません "I'm not going anywhere".

Particles other than が and を go between the question word and も: どこへも, だれにも.
nuances: With a positive verb, some of these mean "every": どこも "everywhere". Learn the negative use first.
何も is read なにも.
common_mistakes: Using a positive verb: 何も食べます ✗ → 何も食べません.
Mixing up 何か (something) and 何も (nothing).

comparisons.note: 何も + negative is "nothing"; 何か is "something".

examples.japanese: 今朝は何も食べませんでした。
examples.furigana: {今朝|けさ}は{何|なに}も{食|た}べませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't eat anything this morning.

examples.japanese: 教室にだれもいません。
examples.furigana: {教室|きょうしつ}にだれもいません。
examples.english: There's no one in the classroom.

examples.japanese: 日曜日はどこへも行きませんでした。
examples.furigana: {日曜日|にちようび}はどこへも{行|い}きませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't go anywhere on Sunday.

examples.japanese: 冷蔵庫に何もありません。
examples.furigana: {冷蔵庫|れいぞうこ}に{何|なに}もありません。
examples.english: There's nothing in the fridge.

examples.japanese: 昨日はだれにも会いませんでした。
examples.furigana: {昨日|きのう}はだれにも{会|あ}いませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't see anyone yesterday.

points.title: あまり／全然 + negative
structure: あまり + negative
全然 + negative
points.explanation:
あまり with a negative softens it to "not very" or "not much": あまり高くないです, "It's not very expensive." 全然 with a negative makes it total: 全然わかりません, "I don't understand at all."

Both need a negative verb or adjective to finish the thought.
nuances: In casual speech 全然 sometimes appears with positive words (全然大丈夫, "totally fine"), but stick to negatives for now.
あんまり is a casual form of あまり.
common_mistakes: Using あまり with a positive: あまり高いです ✗ → あまり高くないです.
Reading あまり as "too much" — that meaning belongs to 〜すぎる, a later lesson.

examples.japanese: この店はあまり高くないです。
examples.furigana: この{店|みせ}はあまり{高|たか}くないです。
examples.english: This shop isn't very expensive.

examples.japanese: 英語が全然わかりません。
examples.furigana: {英語|えいご}が{全然|ぜんぜん}わかりません。
examples.english: I don't understand English at all.

examples.japanese: 肉はあまり食べません。
examples.furigana: {肉|にく}はあまり{食|た}べません。
examples.english: I don't eat much meat.

examples.japanese: 昨日は全然寝ませんでした。
examples.furigana: {昨日|きのう}は{全然|ぜんぜん}{寝|ね}ませんでした。
examples.english: I didn't sleep at all yesterday.

examples.japanese: テレビはあまり見ません。
examples.furigana: テレビはあまり{見|み}ません。
examples.english: I don't watch TV much.

points.title: ごろ／ぐらい
structure: Point in time + ごろ
Amount / length of time + ぐらい (くらい)
points.explanation:
ごろ attaches to a point in time: 七時ごろ, "around seven o'clock". ぐらい (also くらい) attaches to amounts and lengths of time: 一時間ぐらい "about an hour", 千円ぐらい "about 1,000 yen".

In short: ごろ is for when, ぐらい is for how much or how long.
nuances: ごろ can take に or leave it out: 七時ごろ(に)寝ます.
ぐらい and くらい are interchangeable in most sentences.
common_mistakes: Using ごろ with a length of time: 二時間ごろ ✗ → 二時間ぐらい.
Using ぐらい for a clock time is heard in speech, but ごろ is the standard choice.

examples.japanese: 毎晩十一時ごろ寝ます。
examples.furigana: {毎晩|まいばん}{十一時|じゅういちじ}ごろ{寝|ね}ます。
examples.english: I go to bed around eleven every night.

examples.japanese: 駅まで十分ぐらいです。
examples.furigana: {駅|えき}まで{十分|じゅっぷん}ぐらいです。
examples.english: It's about ten minutes to the station.

examples.japanese: 毎日二時間ぐらい勉強します。
examples.furigana: {毎日|まいにち}{二時間|にじかん}ぐらい{勉強|べんきょう}します。
examples.english: I study for about two hours every day.

examples.japanese: 三時ごろ電話します。
examples.furigana: {三時|さんじ}ごろ{電話|でんわ}します。
examples.english: I'll call around three.

examples.japanese: この本は千円ぐらいでした。
examples.furigana: この{本|ほん}は{千円|せんえん}ぐらいでした。
examples.english: This book was about 1,000 yen.

points.title: Counters (〜つ／〜人／〜枚…)
structure: Number + counter (つ・人・枚・本・冊・匹・台…)
Noun + を + Number + counter + Verb
points.explanation:
Japanese counts with counters that depend on the shape or kind of thing: 〜枚 for flat things (paper, shirts), 〜本 for long thin things (bottles, pens), 〜冊 for books, 〜匹 for small animals, 〜台 for machines, 〜人 for people. The native series ひとつ、ふたつ、みっつ… (〜つ) works for general objects up to ten.

The number and counter usually come after the noun and particle, right before the verb: りんごを三つください, "Three apples, please."
nuances: People: ひとり、ふたり, then さんにん、よにん…
Sound changes are common: いっぽん、にほん、さんぼん; いっさつ; いっぴき、さんびき.
common_mistakes: Using the number alone: 本を三買った ✗ → 本を三冊買った.
Saying いちにん／ににん for one or two people — it's ひとり／ふたり.

examples.japanese: りんごを三つください。
examples.furigana: りんごを{三|みっ}つください。
examples.english: Three apples, please.

examples.japanese: 教室に学生が五人います。
examples.furigana: {教室|きょうしつ}に{学生|がくせい}が{五人|ごにん}います。
examples.english: There are five students in the classroom.

examples.japanese: 切手を二枚買いました。
examples.furigana: {切手|きって}を{二枚|にまい}{買|か}いました。
examples.english: I bought two stamps.

examples.japanese: ビールを一本飲みました。
examples.furigana: ビールを{一本|いっぽん}{飲|の}みました。
examples.english: I drank one bottle of beer.

examples.japanese: 兄弟が二人います。
examples.furigana: {兄弟|きょうだい}が{二人|ふたり}います。
examples.english: I have two brothers and sisters.

examples.japanese: 先週、本を三冊読みました。
examples.furigana: {先週|せんしゅう}、{本|ほん}を{三冊|さんさつ}{読|よ}みました。
examples.english: Last week I read three books.

points.title: 〜中 (ちゅう／じゅう)
points.meaning: in the middle of (ちゅう) / all through (じゅう)
structure: Noun + 中 (ちゅう): in progress (仕事中, 会議中)
Time / place + 中 (じゅう): all through (一日中, 世界中)
points.explanation: 中 has two readings. As ちゅう, it means something is in progress: 父は今、仕事中です, "My father's at work right now." As じゅう, it means "all through" a time or place: 一日中雨でした, "It rained all day." 世界中で人気があります, "It's popular all over the world."
nuances: Signs use the ちゅう reading: 準備中 (getting ready), 営業中 (open).
今日中に (きょうじゅうに) means "by the end of today".
common_mistakes: Mixing up the readings: 一日中 is いちにちじゅう, not いちにちちゅう.
Using 中 for a single moment rather than an ongoing state.

examples.japanese: 父は今、仕事中です。
examples.furigana: {父|ちち}は{今|いま}、{仕事|しごと}{中|ちゅう}です。
examples.english: My father's at work right now.

examples.japanese: 昨日は一日中雨でした。
examples.furigana: {昨日|きのう}は{一日|いちにち}{中|じゅう}{雨|あめ}でした。
examples.english: It rained all day yesterday.

examples.japanese: この歌は世界中で人気があります。
examples.furigana: この{歌|うた}は{世界|せかい}{中|じゅう}で{人気|にんき}があります。
examples.english: This song is popular all over the world.

examples.japanese: 部長は会議中です。
examples.furigana: {部長|ぶちょう}は{会議|かいぎ}{中|ちゅう}です。
examples.english: The manager is in a meeting.

examples.japanese: 夏休み中に国へ帰ります。
examples.furigana: {夏休|なつやす}み{中|ちゅう}に{国|くに}へ{帰|かえ}ります。
examples.english: I'll go back to my country during the summer break.

points.title: だけ
structure: Noun / number + だけ
points.explanation:
だけ means "only" or "just" and follows the word it limits: 水だけ飲みます "I only drink water", 一つだけ "just one".

が and を are usually dropped after だけ, or come after it: 水だけを飲みます is also fine.
nuances: だけ simply states a limit. しか〜ない, a later lesson, stresses that it's less than hoped.
Other particles can come before or after だけ: 日曜日にだけ / 日曜日だけに.
common_mistakes: Putting だけ before the noun: だけ水 ✗ → 水だけ.
Using だけ with a negative to mean "only" — that's しか: 水しか飲みません.

examples.japanese: 朝はコーヒーだけ飲みます。
examples.furigana: {朝|あさ}はコーヒーだけ{飲|の}みます。
examples.english: In the morning I only have coffee.

examples.japanese: 一つだけください。
examples.furigana: {一|ひと}つだけください。
examples.english: Just one, please.

examples.japanese: 日曜日だけ休みです。
examples.furigana: {日曜日|にちようび}だけ{休|やす}みです。
examples.english: Only Sundays are days off.

examples.japanese: 日本語は少しだけわかります。
examples.furigana: {日本語|にほんご}は{少|すこ}しだけわかります。
examples.english: I understand just a little Japanese.

examples.japanese: 今日は五分だけ走りました。
examples.furigana: {今日|きょう}は{五分|ごふん}だけ{走|はし}りました。
examples.english: Today I ran for only five minutes.

points.title: Verb-たい
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + たい
Polite: 〜たいです
Negative: 〜たくない(です)
Past: 〜たかった(です)
points.explanation:
Attach たい to the ます-stem to say you want to do something: 行きます → 行きたい, "I want to go."

The result behaves like an い-adjective. Add です to make it polite (行きたいです), and conjugate it like one: 行きたくないです (don't want to go), 行きたかったです (wanted to go). The object can be marked with を or が: 水を飲みたい / 水が飲みたい.
nuances: たい describes your own wishes. Stating someone else's (田中さんは行きたいです) sounds like mind-reading; Japanese uses other forms for that, except in questions.
Asking a superior 〜たいですか directly can feel intrusive. Softer phrasing comes later.
To want a thing rather than an action, use ほしい, not たい.
common_mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 行くたい ✗ → 行きたい.
Using たい with a noun: 車がたいです ✗ → 車がほしいです.
Adding だ: 行きたいだ ✗ — like any い-adjective it doesn't take だ.

examples.japanese: 京都へ行きたいです。
examples.furigana: {京都|きょうと}へ{行|い}きたいです。
examples.english: I want to go to Kyoto.

examples.japanese: 冷たい水を飲みたいです。
examples.furigana: {冷|つめ}たい{水|みず}を{飲|の}みたいです。
examples.english: I want to drink some cold water.

examples.japanese: 今日は何を食べたいですか。
examples.furigana: {今日|きょう}は{何|なに}を{食|た}べたいですか。
examples.english: What do you want to eat today?

examples.japanese: 日本で働きたいです。
examples.furigana: {日本|にほん}で{働|はたら}きたいです。
examples.english: I want to work in Japan.

examples.japanese: 今日は勉強したくないです。
examples.furigana: {今日|きょう}は{勉強|べんきょう}したくないです。
examples.english: I don't want to study today.
examples.hint: する (to do) → don't want to

examples.japanese: 日曜日は家でゆっくり休みたいです。
examples.furigana: {日曜日|にちようび}は{家|いえ}でゆっくり{休|やす}みたいです。
examples.english: On Sunday I want to relax at home.

points.title: 〜がほしい
structure: Noun + が + ほしい(です)
Negative: ほしくない(です)
Past: ほしかった(です)
points.explanation:
ほしい means "want" for things: 新しい車がほしいです, "I want a new car." The thing you want takes が. ほしい is an い-adjective, so it conjugates like one: ほしくない, ほしかった.

For wanting to do something, use 〜たい instead.
nuances: Like たい, ほしい describes your own wishes. Saying someone else wants something needs another form (ほしがっている), covered later.
Asking a superior 〜がほしいですか can sound too direct.
common_mistakes: Mixing up ほしい (a thing) and たい (an action): 車がたいです ✗ → 車がほしいです.
Treating ほしい like a verb: ほしいません ✗ → ほしくないです.

comparisons.note: ほしい is for things (車がほしい); たい is for actions (車を買いたい).

examples.japanese: 新しいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.furigana: {新|あたら}しいパソコンがほしいです。
examples.english: I want a new computer.

examples.japanese: 誕生日に何がほしいですか。
examples.furigana: {誕生日|たんじょうび}に{何|なに}がほしいですか。
examples.english: What do you want for your birthday?

examples.japanese: 今は何もほしくないです。
examples.furigana: {今|いま}は{何|なに}もほしくないです。
examples.english: I don't want anything right now.

examples.japanese: 子どものとき、犬がほしかったです。
examples.furigana: {子|こ}どものとき、{犬|いぬ}がほしかったです。
examples.english: When I was a kid, I wanted a dog.

examples.japanese: もっと時間がほしいです。
examples.furigana: もっと{時間|じかん}がほしいです。
examples.english: I want more time.

points.title: 〜ませんか
points.meaning: Won't you…? / Would you like to…? — invitations
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ませんか
points.explanation:
A negative question is the polite way to invite someone: 一緒に映画を見ませんか, "Would you like to see a movie with me?" Literally it's "Won't you see…?", which leaves the other person free to say no.

It's softer and more considerate than ましょう (let's).
nuances: A typical yes: いいですね。行きましょう。 A soft no: すみません、ちょっと…
It also works for polite offers: お茶を飲みませんか, "Would you like some tea?"
common_mistakes: Inviting with 〜たいですか ("Do you want to…?"), which sounds nosy → 〜ませんか.
Turning down an invitation with a plain いいえ sounds blunt. ちょっと… is gentler.

comparisons.note: ませんか asks; ましょう proposes. ませんか leaves room to decline.

examples.japanese: 一緒に映画を見ませんか。
examples.furigana: {一緒|いっしょ}に{映画|えいが}を{見|み}ませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to watch a movie together?

valid_alternatives.note: 見ましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.
みましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.

examples.japanese: 週末、海へ行きませんか。
examples.furigana: {週末|しゅうまつ}、{海|うみ}へ{行|い}きませんか。
examples.english: How about going to the beach this weekend?

valid_alternatives.note: 行きましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.
いきましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.

examples.japanese: お茶を飲みませんか。
examples.furigana: お{茶|ちゃ}を{飲|の}みませんか。
examples.english: Would you like some tea?

examples.japanese: 今晩、一緒に晩ご飯を食べませんか。
examples.furigana: {今晩|こんばん}、{一緒|いっしょ}に{晩|ばん}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べませんか。
examples.english: Would you like to have dinner together tonight?

valid_alternatives.note: 食べましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.
たべましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.

examples.japanese: 明日、テニスをしませんか。
examples.furigana: {明日|あした}、テニスをしませんか。
examples.english: Want to play tennis tomorrow?

valid_alternatives.note: しましょう is also a natural invitation, but more assertive. This review wants the softer ませんか.

points.title: 〜ましょう
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ましょう
points.explanation:
Replace ます with ましょう to say "let's": 行きましょう, "Let's go." Use it to propose doing something together, and as a warm reply to an invitation: いいですね、行きましょう.

It's more assertive than 〜ませんか, which leaves room for a no.
nuances: Teachers and signs use ましょう for gentle instructions: 手を洗いましょう, "Let's wash our hands."
The casual version is the volitional form (行こう), coming at N4.
common_mistakes: Using ましょう to invite someone you're unsure about — ませんか is more considerate.
Adding です: 行きましょうです ✗.

examples.japanese: 少し休みましょう。
examples.furigana: {少|すこ}し{休|やす}みましょう。
examples.english: Let's take a short break.

points.title: 〜ましょうか
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + ましょうか
points.explanation:
Adding か to ましょう makes an offer or a suggestion: 窓を開けましょうか, "Shall I open the window?" 何時に会いましょうか, "What time shall we meet?"

Context decides whether it means "Shall I…" (offering help) or "Shall we…" (planning together).
nuances: Accept an offer with ええ、お願いします; decline politely with いいえ、大丈夫です.
With a question word it asks for a decision: どこで食べましょうか.
common_mistakes: Confusing ましょうか and ませんか. ませんか invites the other person to do something; ましょうか offers your help or plans together.
Offering help with 〜たいですか, which sounds like you're asking about their wishes.

comparisons.note: ませんか invites the listener; ましょうか offers or plans.

examples.japanese: 窓を開けましょうか。
examples.furigana: {窓|まど}を{開|あ}けましょうか。
examples.english: Shall I open the window?

points.title: 〜に行く／来る (purpose)
points.meaning: go / come in order to do something
structure: Verb (ます-stem) + に + 行く / 来る / 帰る
Activity noun + に + 行く (買い物に行く)
points.explanation:
To say why you're going somewhere, put the ます-stem before に and a movement verb: 映画を見に行きます, "I'm going to see a movie." With nouns that name an activity, the noun takes に directly: 買い物に行きます, "I'm going shopping."

The destination can appear too, marked with へ or に: 図書館へ本を借りに行きます.
nuances: The stem is the same one you use before ます: 食べ, 飲み, 見, し.
It works with 来る and 帰る as well: 昼ご飯を食べに帰ります.
common_mistakes: Using the dictionary form: 見るに行きます ✗ → 見に行きます.
Using で for the purpose: 買い物で行きます ✗ → 買い物に行きます.

points.title: もう／まだ
points.meaning: already, no longer / still, not yet
structure: もう + past (already)
もう + negative (no longer)
まだ + positive (still)
いいえ、まだです (not yet)
points.explanation:
もう with a past verb means "already": もう食べました, "I've already eaten." With a negative it means "no longer": もう痛くないです, "It doesn't hurt anymore."

まだ with a positive means "still": まだ雨です, "It's still raining." The short answer いいえ、まだです means "No, not yet."
nuances: The full "not yet" sentence uses 〜ていません (まだ食べていません), which comes with the て-form lessons.
もう also means "more" before a number: もう一つ, "one more".
common_mistakes: まだ食べませんでした ✗ for "I haven't eaten yet" → まだです / まだ食べていません.
Mixing up もう (already) and まだ (still / not yet).

examples.japanese: もう昼ご飯を食べましたか。
examples.furigana: もう{昼|ひる}ご{飯|はん}を{食|た}べましたか。
examples.english: Have you had lunch already?

examples.japanese: いいえ、まだです。
examples.furigana: いいえ、まだです。
examples.english: No, not yet.

examples.japanese: 外はまだ雨です。
examples.furigana: {外|そと}はまだ{雨|あめ}です。

points.title: Adverbs: 〜く／〜に
structure: い-adjective: drop い → く (早い → 早く)
な-adjective + に (静か → 静かに)
いい → よく
points.explanation:
To describe how an action is done, turn an adjective into an adverb. い-adjectives change い to く: 早い → 早く起きます, "get up early". な-adjectives take に: 静か → 静かに話します, "speak quietly".

The adverb goes before the verb it describes.
nuances: いい becomes よく: よく寝ました, "I slept well." よく also means "often".
The same く／に forms appear with なる (become), the next lesson.
common_mistakes: Using the plain adjective: 早い起きます ✗ → 早く起きます.
Using な instead of に: 静かな話します ✗ → 静かに話します.

examples.japanese: 明日は早く起きます。
examples.furigana: {明日|あした}は{早|はや}く{起|お}きます。

points.title: 〜くなる／〜になる
structure: い-adjective: drop い → くなる
な-adjective / Noun + になる
points.explanation: なる means "become". With い-adjectives, change い to く: 寒い → 寒くなりました, "It's gotten cold." With な-adjectives and nouns, use に: 元気になりました "I got better", 先生になりたいです "I want to become a teacher".
nuances: The past なりました often describes a change you've just noticed: 暗くなりました, "It's gotten dark."
Seasons, times and ages use に: 春になりました, 二十歳になりました.
common_mistakes: Using に with an い-adjective: 寒いになります ✗ → 寒くなります.
Dropping に after a noun: 先生なりたい ✗ → 先生になりたい.

comparisons.note: になる: something becomes X. にする: you choose or make it X.

examples.english: It's gotten cold, hasn't it?

examples.japanese: 春になりました。

points.title: AはBより
structure: A + は + B + より + adjective
points.explanation:
より means "than". In A は B より 高い, A is the thing described and B is the point of comparison: 東京は大阪より大きいです, "Tokyo is bigger than Osaka."

Japanese adjectives have no comparative form like English "-er". より does all the work.
nuances: Add ずっと (much) or 少し (a little): 東京は大阪よりずっと大きいです.
より can also come first, with のほうが: 大阪より東京のほうが大きい — the next lessons.
common_mistakes: Swapping the roles: the noun before より is the one that is less.
Looking for a comparative ending: 大きいより ✗ — the adjective stays as it is.

examples.japanese: 東京は大阪より大きいです。
examples.furigana: {東京|とうきょう}は{大阪|おおさか}より{大|おお}きいです。
examples.english: Tokyo is bigger than Osaka.

examples.furigana: {今日|きょう}は{昨日|きのう}より{寒|さむ}いです。

examples.japanese: 電車はバスより速いです。
examples.furigana: {電車|でんしゃ}はバスより{速|はや}いです。
examples.english: Trains are faster than buses.

examples.japanese: 兄は私より三つ上です。

examples.furigana: この{本|ほん}はあの{本|ほん}よりおもしろいです。

points.title: AとBとどちらが
points.meaning: Which is more …, A or B?
structure: A + と + B + と + どちらが + adjective + ですか
Answer: A + のほうが + adjective + です
points.explanation:
To ask which of two things is more something, list both with と and ask with どちらが: 犬と猫とどちらが好きですか, "Which do you like more, dogs or cats?"

どちら is the question word for a choice between two. The answer usually uses のほうが, the next lesson.
nuances: どっち is the casual form of どちら.
If both are equal: どちらも好きです, "I like both."
common_mistakes: Using どれ for two options: どれが ✗ → どちらが.
Using は after どちら: どちらは ✗ — question words take が.

examples.furigana: {犬|いぬ}と{猫|ねこ}とどちらが{好|す}きですか。
examples.english: Which do you like more, dogs or cats?

examples.japanese: 電車とバスとどちらが速いですか。
examples.furigana: {電車|でんしゃ}とバスとどちらが{速|はや}いですか。

examples.furigana: コーヒーと{紅茶|こうちゃ}とどちらがいいですか。

points.title: 〜のほうが
structure: A + のほうが + adjective
B + より + A + のほうが + adjective
points.explanation:
のほうが picks one side of a comparison: 猫のほうが好きです, "I prefer cats." It's the natural answer to a どちら question.

Add より to name the other side: 犬より猫のほうが好きです, "I like cats more than dogs."
nuances: ほう literally means "side" or "direction".
Adjectives can come before ほう directly: 安いほうがいいです, "The cheaper one is better."
common_mistakes: Dropping の after a noun: 猫ほうが ✗ → 猫のほうが.
Answering with は: 猫のほうは… sounds like a contrast, not an answer.

comparisons.note: A は B より puts A first as the topic; B より A のほうが is the usual answer to どちら.

examples.japanese: 猫のほうが好きです。
examples.furigana: {猫|ねこ}のほうが{好|す}きです。
examples.english: I prefer cats.

examples.furigana: {電車|でんしゃ}のほうが{速|はや}いです。
examples.english: The train is faster.

examples.furigana: {夏|なつ}より{冬|ふゆ}のほうが{好|す}きです。
examples.english: I like winter more than summer.

examples.furigana: バスより{自転車|じてんしゃ}のほうが{便利|べんり}です。
examples.english: A bicycle is more convenient than the bus.

examples.japanese: こっちのほうが安いです。
examples.furigana: こっちのほうが{安|やす}いです。
examples.english: This one is cheaper.

points.title: 〜で一番
structure: Group / place + で + 一番 + adjective
Group + の中で + 何 / だれ / どこ + が + 一番 …
points.explanation:
一番 (いちばん) before an adjective makes a superlative: 一番高い, "the most expensive" or "the tallest". The group or range goes before で: 日本で一番高い山, "the tallest mountain in Japan".

To ask, use a question word with が: 果物の中で何が一番好きですか, "Which fruit do you like best?"
nuances: の中で (among) is used when the group is a list or category.
一番 on its own means "number one" or "first".
common_mistakes: Using に for the range: 日本に一番高い山 ✗ → 日本で一番高い山.
Putting 一番 after the adjective: 高い一番 ✗.

examples.english: Which fruit do you like best?

points.title: て-form: る-verbs (ichidan)
points.meaning: do A and (then) B — る-verbs drop る and add て
structure: る-verbs: drop る + て
食べる → 食べて, 見る → 見て, 起きる → 起きて
Verb て、Verb — the tense comes from the last verb
points.explanation:
The て-form joins actions in the order they happen: 朝ご飯を食べて、学校へ行きます, "I eat breakfast and go to school." The tense comes only from the last verb.

The て-form is built differently for each verb group, so it's split into six short lessons. This one is the easy group, る-verbs (ichidan): drop る and add て. 食べる → 食べて, 見る → 見て, 寝る → 寝て.

It's also the building block for many patterns ahead — てください, ています, てもいい — so it's worth drilling until it's automatic.
nuances: Most verbs ending in -iru or -eru are る-verbs: 見る, 起きる, 着る, 寝る, 食べる, 開ける.
Some look like る-verbs but are う-verbs: 帰る, 入る, 走る, 知る. They take って (帰って), which comes in the next lesson.
common_mistakes: 食べって ✗ → 食べて: る-verbs never add a small っ.
Putting the past tense on the first verb: 食べました、学校へ行きました is two sentences; to join them, use 食べて、学校へ行きました.
